screens.title: Introduction to OOP — Classes and Objects
screens.subtitle: Model real-world entities in Java using classes, fields, methods, and instances

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how Java models the real world using objects built from class blueprints. We will use simple analogies like a house blueprint or a cookie cutter to make the ideas concrete, and then walk through short Java examples that show how to declare a class, give it fields and methods, create instances with the new keyword, and access members with the dot operator. You will see a Dog example and a small main program that creates two distinct Dog objects with different states. Understanding these basics matters because they are the entry point to encapsulation, reuse, and modular design in Java. A common beginner mistake is to confuse a class with an object; we will show why the class is a template and objects are the concrete instances you can manipulate. By the end you will be able to read a class definition, instantiate objects, and call methods on those objects with confidence.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A class is a blueprint; an object is a concrete instance with its own state and behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: These objectives set specific, verifiable skills you will gain. First, you will explain the fundamental principles and benefits of object-oriented programming, which means naming the paradigm and saying why it helps structure programs. Second, you will differentiate between classes and objects: describe a class as a blueprint and an object as a concrete instance with its own state. Third, you will define a class in Java by declaring instance variables and methods, and explain what fields and methods represent. Fourth, you will create objects using the new keyword and access fields and methods with the dot operator. Each objective is paired with small practice checks so you can confirm competency. For example, you should be able to read a short Dog class and point to which lines declare fields versus methods, then write two lines that create objects and set their names. These skills matter because they are the building blocks for encapsulation and modular design in Java.

screens.title: What is Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)?
screens.subtitle: A practical definition and why Java uses it

narration.text: Object-oriented programming is a way of organizing software where the primary units are objects: bundles of state and behavior. In Java, objects hold their data in fields and define actions as methods. This structure lets you model concrete things like a car or a dog in code by creating a class that specifies the attributes and behaviors, then making many independent instances. For example, a Dog class defines name, breed, and age; each Dog object stores its own values for these fields and can run the same bark or eat methods. One practical benefit is modularity: by grouping related data and behavior inside a class you reduce accidental coupling between unrelated parts of a program. Another is reuse: a well-designed class can be used in multiple programs or extended later. A common misconception is that OOP always makes code more complex. In fact, when used correctly, it simplifies maintenance by localizing changes to the relevant class. To test your understanding, imagine replacing fields in a class — ask whether the change affects every object or only new instances. That question reveals the object-instance distinction at the heart of OOP.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: OOP organizes programs around objects that combine state (fields) and behavior (methods), mapped from real-world entities.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is OOP?
Objects bundle state and behavior so code models real-world entities in a modular way.
  • • Objects contain fields (data) and methods (behavior).
  • • Classes define the shape and actions; objects are the concrete instances.
  • • Java uses classes and objects to implement encapsulation and reuse.
  • • Modularity reduces accidental coupling and helps maintenance.
Takeaway
Think in terms of entities: design a class once and create multiple independent objects from it.
Analogy: Blueprint and House
The blueprint is the class. Each house built from it is an object with its own paint color and furniture.
Example scenario
A Dog class describes name and age. Two Dog objects hold different names and ages but share the same methods like bark().
Common mistake
Confusing a class with an object. You cannot set instance values on a class itself; values belong to objects created from the class.

screens.title: Classes: blueprints that define fields and methods
screens.subtitle: What goes inside a Java class and why each piece matters

narration.text: A class in Java is a blueprint that defines the data an object will store and the operations it can perform. Fields, also called instance variables, represent attributes such as name, breed, or age. Methods encapsulate behavior like bark or eat. Declaring them inside a class groups related code and prevents unrelated parts of the program from touching internal state directly. For example, a simple Dog class has String name, String breed, and int age fields, and methods public void bark() and public void eat(String food). The keywords like public are access modifiers that control visibility, but the essential idea for now is that fields hold state per object and methods perform actions that may read or modify that state. One misconception is thinking that methods belong to an object only if you create it; methods are defined by the class and are available to every instance. Another misconception is treating fields like global variables: fields are tied to individual objects unless declared static. Check your understanding by asking: when I change a field on myDog, which other objects are affected? The correct answer is none — only that specific object changes.

keyIdea.title: Class anatomy
keyIdea.text: Classes contain fields for state and methods for behavior; fields belong to instances and methods define shared behavior.

content.html:
Definition
What a class contains
Fields declare the data each object will carry. Methods define the actions any instance can perform.
  • • Fields (instance variables): per-object state like name and age.
  • • Methods: code that acts on an object's state or performs operations.
  • • Access modifiers control visibility; focus on public for now.
Key Takeaway
Fields store unique data per instance; methods provide behavior available to every instance defined by the class.
Concrete Example: Dog class
This example shows fields and methods placed inside a class body.
public class Dog {
    String name;
    String breed;
    int age;

    public void bark() {
        System.out.println(name + " says Woof!");
    }

    public void eat(String food) {
        System.out.println(name + " is eating " + food + ".");
    }
}
Misconception
Fields are not shared between separate objects unless declared static. Each object has its own copy of instance fields.

screens.title: Reading a Dog class and a Kennel main method
screens.subtitle: See how objects are created and used in a short program

narration.text: Let's walk through a small Java program that defines a Dog class and a Kennel with a main method that creates Dog objects. The class lists instance variables for name, breed, and age, and methods like bark and eat. In main, we use new to create objects: Dog myDog = new Dog(); This line does two things: it creates a new Dog instance in memory and assigns a reference to the variable myDog. We then set fields with statements like myDog. name = "Buddy"; and call behavior with myDog. bark(). Notice how each object stores its own values: myDog. name and yourDog. name can be different. A common beginner error is to omit new and think the declaration alone creates an object. Another subtle point is that methods are declared in the class and invoked on instances; the same bark method runs for each object but uses that object's name when printing. To confirm understanding, read the code and predict the printed lines before running the program. Reading a Dog class and a Kennel main method means use new classname() to make an object; assign fields and call methods with the dot operator to act on that object.. In practical terms, see how objects are created and used in a short program. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Use new ClassName() to make an object; assign fields and call methods with the dot operator to act on that object.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Dog and Kennel example
Read the code and predict output before running it to deepen understanding.
public class Dog {
    String name;
    String breed;
    int age;

    public void bark() {
        System.out.println(name + " says Woof!");
    }

    public void eat(String food) {
        System.out.println(name + " is eating " + food + ".");
    }
}

public class Kennel {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Dog myDog = new Dog();
        myDog.name = "Buddy";
        myDog.breed = "Golden Retriever";
        myDog.age = 3;
        myDog.bark();
        myDog.eat("kibble");

        Dog yourDog = new Dog();
        yourDog.name = "Lucy";
        yourDog.bark();
    }
}
Supporting notes
  • • Declaration vs instantiation: Dog myDog; only declares a reference. Dog myDog = new Dog(); actually creates an object.
  • • Setting fields assigns object state for that instance only.
  • • Calling a method like bark() uses that instance's fields inside the method body.
Check your understanding
Before running, predict what lines will print. Then run and compare.

screens.title: Instantiation: steps to create and use an object
screens.subtitle: A numbered process you can follow every time

narration.text: Instantiating and using an object follows a simple, reliable sequence you can memorize and apply. First, declare a reference variable to hold the object's reference. For example, write Dog myDog; This reserves a named reference but does not create an object. Second, create the object using the new keyword with a constructor call: myDog = new Dog(); This allocates an instance and returns its reference. Third, initialize the instance by assigning its fields explicitly or by calling methods that set state. For example, myDog. name = "Buddy"; Fourth, invoke behavior on the object with the dot operator, such as myDog. bark(); That runs the method logic using the instance's current state. A typical beginner error is skipping the new step and trying to access fields on a null reference. Another subtle point is that constructors establish initial state; when you see empty parentheses after the class name you are invoking a default constructor. Practice these steps until they feel like a routine: declare, new, initialize, call. Then ask: if I change a field on myDog, did I change yourDog? No — each instance keeps its own state.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation steps
keyIdea.text: Declare a reference, use new to create an object, initialize its fields, and call methods with the dot operator.

content.html:
Process Flow
How to instantiate and use an object
Follow these four steps every time you create and use an object.
Common error: forgetting new
1. Declare
Dog myDog;
2. Instantiate
myDog = new Dog();
3. Initialize
myDog.name = "Buddy";
4. Call
myDog.bark();
Why each step matters
  • • Declaration creates a reference variable type-checked by the compiler.
  • • new actually creates the object in memory and returns its reference.
  • • Initialization sets the instance's fields so methods can rely on valid data.
  • • Calling methods runs behavior that uses the object's state.

screens.title: Methods: defining behavior and parameters
screens.subtitle: How methods operate on instance state and accept inputs

narration.text: Methods are named blocks of code inside a class that describe what an object can do. They can access and modify the instance fields of the object they run on. For example, public void eat(String food) receives a food parameter and can use the object's name field to print a message that includes which dog is eating. Methods can be parameterless or accept one or more parameters and may return values, but in our Dog example we use void methods that perform actions and print output. One important idea is that the same method body is shared across objects; it runs using the calling object's state. A common misconception is thinking methods are copied per object; they are defined once by the class and executed in the context of each instance. To practice, imagine two objects calling the same method with different field values — the behavior will reflect each object's state. A short code snippet highlights this relationship and shows how parameters let methods receive input without changing the caller's variable unless explicitly assigned inside the method. Methods: defining behavior and parameters means methods implement behavior that acts on an object's fields; parameters let callers pass information into those behaviors.. In practical terms, how methods operate on instance state and accept inputs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Method role
keyIdea.text: Methods implement behavior that acts on an object's fields; parameters let callers pass information into those behaviors.

content.html:
Definition
Methods and parameters
Methods operate on an instance's fields and can accept parameters to receive input.
  • • Methods are defined in the class and executed on instances.
  • • Parameters are local names for values passed in at call time.
  • • Methods can change an object's fields, affecting that instance's state.
Pro tip
Keep method responsibilities focused: a method should do one clear action on the object's data.
Code example
public void eat(String food) {
    System.out.println(name + " is eating " + food + ".");
}

// Called as:
myDog.eat("kibble");
yourDog.eat("treats");
Each call passes a different argument. The same method uses the calling object's name field to produce different printed lines.
Misconception
Passing a variable into a method does not silently change the caller's variable unless the method explicitly assigns to a field or returns a new value that you assign back.

screens.title: Objects compared: myDog vs yourDog
screens.subtitle: How two instances of the same class remain independent

narration.text: Comparing two objects clarifies how instance state is stored and used. Suppose we create Dog myDog and Dog yourDog from the same Dog class. Both share the same fields and methods in definition, but each object holds its own values for name, breed, and age. When myDog. name is set to Buddy and yourDog. name to Lucy, calling myDog. bark() prints Buddy says Woof!, while yourDog. bark() prints Lucy says Woof!. This demonstrates state isolation: operations on one object do not change the other's fields. Beginners sometimes expect that changing a field on one instance will reflect on all instances; that only happens for static fields shared at the class level. Another contrast is between objects and primitive variables: updating an int variable changes that value directly, but updating an object reference variable can make it point to a different object. To test yourself, create two objects and change a field on one. Then ask which objects reflect the change and why. This small experiment reinforces the distinction between class-level definitions and instance-level state. Objects compared: myDog vs yourDog means separate objects created from the same class each maintain independent field values and behaviors.. In practical terms, how two instances of the same class remain independent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: State isolation
keyIdea.text: Separate objects created from the same class each maintain independent field values and behaviors.

Comparison
myDog vs yourDog
Same class, different instance state.
Try setting different names and calling bark()

name = "Buddy"
bark() → prints "Buddy says Woof!"

screens.title: Beginner pitfalls: forgetting new and confusing class vs instance
screens.subtitle: Errors you will see and how to avoid them

narration.text: Two mistakes beginners commonly make are forgetting the new keyword and treating a class like an object. If you declare Product product1; without using new, product1 holds no object reference and is null. Attempting to set fields or call methods on it will lead to a runtime null pointer error. The safe habit is to both declare and instantiate: Product product1 = new Product(); Another frequent error is trying to access instance fields on the class itself. For example, you cannot write Dog. name = "Buddy" to set a name on all dogs; instance fields belong to objects. A third subtle point is the difference between declaration order and assignment: product1 must be declared before it can be assigned. If you swap the order you will produce a compile-time error. To avoid these mistakes, follow the pattern: declare the variable, use new to construct an object, then initialize and call methods. When you see an error, check whether new was used and whether you are trying to access instance fields on the class rather than an instance. Beginner pitfalls: forgetting new and confusing class vs instance means always use new to create objects and remember instance fields belong to objects, not to the class itself.. In practical terms, errors you will see and how to avoid them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls
keyIdea.text: Always use new to create objects and remember instance fields belong to objects, not to the class itself.

content.html:
Common Mistakes
Forgetting new
If you declare a reference without new, the reference points to nothing until you instantiate an object.
Error pattern
Product product1; product1.name = "Laptop"; // causes error until product1 = new Product();
Class vs Instance
Do not assign instance fields on the class
Instance fields live on objects. Changing a field on one instance does not alter other instances.
Quick check
If multiple objects show the same unexpected field value, check for accidental use of static fields or shared references instead of separate instances.

narration.text: The hands-on activity asks you to design a Book class to practice fields, methods, and object behavior checks. Your Book should have title, author, isbn, and isBorrowed fields. Implement displayBookInfo() to print these fields, borrowBook() to set isBorrowed true only when the book is not already borrowed, and returnBook() to set isBorrowed false only when it is currently borrowed. The Library main program should create at least two Book objects, set their fields, and call the methods to demonstrate borrowing and returning logic including the edge cases: trying to borrow an already borrowed book and trying to return a book that is not borrowed. When you write the code, use clear print messages so your output shows which branch ran. These checks validate both state changes and condition logic. After implementing, run the program and verify the outputs match your expectations for each scenario. If a message is missing or a state doesn't change, inspect whether you correctly updated the object's field and not a separate temporary variable. Implement the Book class — design and rules means design book with fields and methods that enforce correct borrowing state and test edge cases in a library main program.. In practical terms, a guided starter and behavior checks for the activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: How OOP basics map to later topics
screens.subtitle: Why fields, methods, and instantiation prepare you for constructors, access control, and inheritance

narration.text: The basics you learn here — fields, methods, classes, and instantiation — are the foundation for several features you will study next. Constructors are special methods that run when new creates an object, letting you initialize fields in one place. Access modifiers like public and private control whether code outside the class can read or change fields; learning to place fields and methods properly prepares you to apply encapsulation later. Inheritance and polymorphism build on classes: when you master defining a class and creating instances, you can later extend a class to add or override behavior. For example, once Dog is familiar, you might create a ServiceDog subclass with specialized methods. A common misconception is that these advanced features replace the basics; they actually reuse the same mechanisms. Understanding how object state and method calls work now makes learning constructors and inheritance much easier because you already grok the role each class member plays. Consider constructors as the organized approach to initialization and access modifiers as the rules that protect your object's state. How OOP basics map to later topics means fields and methods are the primitives that constructors, access control, and inheritance build upon.. In practical terms, why fields, methods, and instantiation prepare you for constructors, access control, and inheritance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Summarizing the essentials helps retain them. First, a class is a blueprint that defines fields and methods. Remember that a class describes the shape and behavior but is not itself an object you can use. Second, an object is an instance created with new; each object holds its own instance variables so state is isolated across objects. Third, the dot operator accesses an object's members: you set fields and invoke methods on a specific instance using this operator. Keep these three concepts clear and practice with short examples that create two objects from the same class and exercise methods with different data. Ask yourself: when I change a field on one object, do other objects change? If the answer is no, you understand instance state. These ideas are the foundation for constructors, access control, and inheritance in later lessons.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Classes define structure and behavior; objects are instances; use new to create objects and the dot operator to access members.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Key Concepts
Class
A blueprint that defines fields and methods for objects of that type.
Object
An instance created with new that holds its own field values and runs methods.
Dot operator
Use objectName.member to access fields or call methods on that specific instance.
Takeaway

Keep practicing by creating classes and multiple objects to see state isolation and method behavior firsthand.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you code

narration.text: A final quick reference reinforces the essentials. Remember that fields declared in a class become instance data for each object you create. Remember to use new to instantiate an object and assign it to a typed reference variable. And remember the dot operator for accessing fields and invoking methods on that specific instance. Keep these three points in mind as you work through the exercise: they are the everyday habits that prevent the most common errors. When you write code, read aloud the line: "I am creating a new Dog instance and storing it in a variable" — it helps make the instantiation step explicit. These habits will pay off when you reach constructors and access control because the concepts simply reuse the same mechanisms introduced here. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means fields → instance data. new → create object. dot operator → access members on that instance.. In practical terms, three compact reminders before you code. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Quick reference
keyIdea.text: Fields → instance data. new → create object. dot operator → access members on that instance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Quick Reference
Fields
Instance variables that store state for each object created from the class.

Dot operator
Use it to access a specific object's fields and to invoke its methods.
Final Tip
